Given two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] if every element of [MATH: A] is an element of [MATH: B,] we say that [MATH: A] is a subset of [MATH: B,] and we write
[MATH: A \subseteq B.]

Content:
For example, consider the following sets:
[MATH: A = \{ {\color{blue}{1}},{\color{blue}{3}} \}, \qquad B = \{ 1,2,3\}, \qquad C=\{1,2,{\color{red}4}\}]

Content:
Notice that every element of [MATH: A] is also an element of [MATH: B{:}]
[MATH: {\color{blue}{1}}\in B, \qquad {\color{blue}{3}}\in B]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: A] is a subset of [MATH: B,] and we write [MATH: A \subseteq B.]

[MATH: 1 \in B, \qquad 2\in B, \qquad {\color{red}4}\notin B]

Content:
Since [MATH: 4 \notin B,] we have that [MATH: C] is not a subset of [MATH: B,] and we write [MATH: C \not\subseteq B.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we must find the elements of the set [MATH: S.] Solving the given inequality, we have

[MATH: − 3 ≤ 2n + 1|≤ 7; − 4 ≤ 2n|≤ 6; − 2 ≤ n|≤ 3.]

So, [MATH: S] contains all integers between [MATH: -2] and [MATH: 3] (including [MATH: -2] and [MATH: 3]):

[MATH: S = \{ -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 \}]

A set is a subset of [MATH: S] if all its elements are elements of [MATH: S.] With that in mind, let's inspect each option.

  • [MATH: \{ -2,0,4 \}] is not a subset of [MATH: S] because it contains the element [MATH: 4 \notin S. \quad \color{red}\times]

  • [MATH: \{ 0,3 \}] is a subset of [MATH: S. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

  • [MATH: \{ -3,1,3 \}] is not a subset of [MATH: S] because it contains the element [MATH: -3 \notin S. \quad \color{red}\times]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".
